endorsements.title: Texas SB 1188 (89th Legislature), electronic health records and AI disclosure
endorsements.quote: the practitioner is acting within the scope of the practitioner's license, certification, or other authorization to provide health care services in this state, regardless of the use of artificial intelligence;

endorsements.title: Action Guide: Artificial Intelligence (AI)
endorsements.issuer: National Association of Community Health Centers
endorsements.quote: AI implementation must comply with HIPAA (Health Insurance and Portability and Accountability Act), obtain appropriate patient consent, and follow rigorous security practices such as encryption, access controls, and regular audits.

endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: The team should also determine how model output for patients will be documented.

endorsements.title: Principles for augmented intelligence development, deployment, and use
endorsements.quote: AI is used in a manner which directly impacts patient care, access to care, medical decision making, or the medical record, that use of AI should be documented in the medical record.

endorsements.title: Guardrails for GenAI drafted replies in patient portal messaging
endorsements.issuer: Sakr J. npj Digital Medicine 2026;9 (PMID 41942581, doi:10.1038/s41746-026-02621-6)
endorsements.quote: Where systems are designed in ways that predictably encourage automation complacency, governance, not individual vigilance, must carry the corrective burden5.

evidence.title: Usage of and Satisfaction with Artificial Intelligence-Generated Draft Replies to Patient Portal Messages
evidence.outcome: Rate of AI draft use and extent of editing of drafts before sending
evidence.effect: Mean rate of starting a reply with an ART draft was 20.2%; 40% of replies showed little to no editing of the draft. Drafts sometimes contained incorrect or inappropriate content (34.9%, n=15).
evidence.quote: The mean rate of starting with an ART draft was 20.2%, and 40% of replies exhibited little to no editing of the draft.
evidence.sample_unit: pilot users (physicians, nurses, nurse practitioners, medical assistants); 52 survey respondents

evidence.title: Opportunities and risks of artificial intelligence in patient portal messaging in primary care
evidence.outcome: Automation complacency letting erroneous AI-drafted messages reach patients after physician review
evidence.effect: All but one physician sent at least one erroneous response; likelihood of a missed error significantly greater than zero (p<0.001) for each erroneous draft; 90% trusted the tool.
evidence.quote: In this simulated environment, all but one physician ‘sent’ at least one fictitious response to a patient that contained an error.

commentary.bottom_line: No study has tested whether system-level controls or clinician documentation of reasoning reduce erroneous AI-drafted messages reaching patients. Two studies show that the hazard exists, with all but one of 20 physicians sending at least one erroneous draft in a simulation and 40% of replies in a real pilot showing little to no editing.

perspectives.view: No study tests the recommended controls or the documentation practice, so certainty for the practice is rated as no direct evidence. The two available studies are a descriptive pilot of 80 users and a vignette simulation with 20 physicians. They show that the problem occurs but cannot indicate whether governance controls change what reaches patients.

In the simulation, all but one physician sent at least one erroneous response, and the likelihood of a missed error was greater than zero for each erroneous draft (p<0.001). Ninety percent trusted the tool. This pattern suggests individual review may not reliably catch errors, which is consistent with the case for system-level controls, though those controls remain untested.

In a real deployment, users started 20.2% of replies from an AI draft, and 40% of replies showed little to no editing. Drafts sometimes contained incorrect or inappropriate content (34.9%, n=15). These figures suggest limited editing in routine workflow. No study measured the time burden or fidelity of documenting reasoning for high-risk replies.

Texas SB 1188 holds the practitioner to the scope of licensure regardless of AI use. The augmented intelligence principles and the CHAI guide call for documenting AI use or output in the record. These sources set accountability and documentation expectations, but none presents outcome data showing that documentation of reasoning reduces message errors.

The simulation found that 90% of physicians trusted the tool while nearly all sent an erroneous reply. This finding suggests that patient reliance on clinician review may rest on checking that did not always occur. No study measured patient harm, patient trust, or whether patients could reach a human after receiving a flawed reply.

Neither hazard study reports including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients or clinics. Errors in drafted replies may affect patients differently depending on their ability to recognize them, but these studies provide no data on that question.

commentary.research_gap: No study has compared system-level controls, such as required editing, flagging of high-risk drafts, or audit of unedited sends, or a requirement to document reasoning for high-risk replies, against usual clinician review. A pragmatic trial or stepped-wedge evaluation in live portal workflows could measure the rate of erroneous content reaching patients, clinician time per message, documentation fidelity, and patient-reported outcomes, with enrollment that includes safety-net sites and patients with limited English proficiency.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, and neither hazard study reports including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems serving these groups therefore have no evidence on how often drafting errors reach their patients or whether the recommended controls would help them.
